quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [p] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: Hold a hand near your mouth: 'please', 'put' and 'pan' should each push out a small puff of air.
quests.explanation: Close both lips, let pressure build behind them, then open with a quick burst. Your voice stays off until the vowel begins.
quests.textToSpeak: Please put the pan on the stove.
quests.phoneticHint: At the start of a stressed word, English [p] is aspirated, roughly [pʰ]: the burst is followed by a tiny breath before the vowel.
commonMistakes: Releasing no air, which makes the [p] sound like a [b] to English ears

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud at a relaxed speed.
quests.hint: 'pick' and 'paper' begin with [p], but 'up' ends with it. Compare how the two positions feel.
quests.explanation: At the start of a word, open the lips with a puff. At the end, close the lips and stop the air; a soft release is enough, and you should not add a vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll pick up the paper on my way home.
quests.phoneticHint: 'up' is [ʌp]: the sound finishes the moment your lips seal, so 'up the' flows as [ʌp ðə] with no extra [ə] in between.
commonMistakes: Adding a vowel after final [p], as in 'up-uh'
Leaving the lips open so 'up' sounds like 'uh'
Saying the middle of 'paper' with a [b]

quests.instruction: Say it the way you would across a dinner table.
quests.hint: 'pepper' has two [p] sounds, and 'pass' and 'please' each begin with another.
quests.explanation: Between the two syllables of 'pepper' your lips close twice. The second [p] is lighter because the syllable is unstressed, but the lips still seal fully.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you pass me the pepper, please?
quests.phoneticHint: 'pepper' is [ˈpepər]: a strong puff on the first [p], a lighter release on the second.
commonMistakes: Turning the second [p] into [b], as in 'pebber'
Dropping the [p] in 'please' when speaking fast

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [b] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: Feel your throat hum at the start of 'bring', 'bottle' and 'beach'.
quests.explanation: Your lips close as for [p], but your voice is already buzzing when they open. There is no puff of air, only a soft voiced release.
quests.textToSpeak: Bring a bottle of water to the beach.
quests.phoneticHint: [b] is voiced from the first instant: [brɪŋ], not [pʰrɪŋ]. Rest fingertips on your throat to check the vibration.
commonMistakes: Adding a strong puff of air, which makes it [p]-like
Closing the lips so lightly that [b] turns into [v]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [b] steady in every position.
quests.hint: Find [b] beginning 'brother' and 'booked', and again in the middle of 'table'.
quests.explanation: Inside 'table' the lips close firmly in the middle of the word. Keep the voice running through the [b] and into the last syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: My brother booked a table for Saturday.
quests.phoneticHint: 'table' is [ˈteɪbəl]: [b] links straight into a very short [l], so keep the voice on and don't add a vowel between them.
commonMistakes: Making the middle [b] a [v], as in 'tavle'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a quick decision.
quests.hint: 'grab' and 'cab' end with [b]. Listen for the voiced closure that finishes each word.
quests.explanation: For a final [b], keep the voice going as the lips close, then release quietly. The vowel before it is slightly longer than before [p].
quests.textToSpeak: I'll grab a cab before it starts to rain.
quests.phoneticHint: Compare 'cab' [kæb] with 'cap' [kæp]: the vowel in 'cab' is longer and the closure is voiced.

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [t] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: Notice [t] at the start of 'tea', 'too' and 'to', and at the end of 'hot'.
quests.explanation: Touch the tip of your tongue to the ridge just behind your upper front teeth, block the air, then release with a sharp burst. Your voice stays off.
quests.textToSpeak: The tea is too hot to drink.
quests.phoneticHint: Initial [t] before a stressed vowel is aspirated [tʰ]: a small puff, then the vowel. The contact point is the ridge, not the teeth.
commonMistakes: Placing the tongue against the teeth, which gives a heavier, dental [t]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [t] steady in every position.
quests.hint: Final [t] ends 'forgot', 'set', 'last' and 'night'. Hear how the tongue stops the air without a vowel after it.
quests.explanation: At the end of a word, raise the tongue tip to the ridge and stop the air. A full release is optional in fast speech, but the closure must be there.
quests.textToSpeak: I forgot to set the alarm last night.
quests.phoneticHint: 'last night' is [læst naɪt]: the [t] in 'last' is squeezed between [s] and the next word, so it is brief and easy to lose.
commonMistakes: Deleting the final [t], so 'night' sounds like 'nigh'
Ending 'last' with [s] only, leaving out the [t]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as if you were giving directions.
quests.hint: [t] appears at the start, in the middle, and at the end of words. Count how many you can hear in 'traffic' and 'station'.
quests.explanation: Keep the tongue tip on the ridge each time. In 'traffic' and 'station' the [t] is part of a cluster, so the tongue must move quickly into [r] or after [s].
quests.textToSpeak: Turn left after the traffic lights and stop at the station.
quests.phoneticHint: 'traffic' [ˈtræfɪk] begins with [tr]: the [t] is released straight into [r], with a hint of friction, and no vowel between.
commonMistakes: Tapping or rolling the [r] after [t] in 'traffic'
Leaving out [t] in 'station', so it sounds like 'sation'
Using a dental [t] with the tongue on the teeth

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [d] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: [d] begins 'dinner', sits inside 'ready', and ends 'Dad'.
quests.explanation: Place your tongue where you did for [t], but turn your voice on before you release, and let out no puff of air.
quests.textToSpeak: Dinner is ready, Dad.
quests.phoneticHint: 'ready' is [ˈredi]: many speakers make the middle [d] a very quick tap, which is fine. What matters is that the voice doesn't switch off.
commonMistakes: Adding a puff of air, which makes it [t]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [d] steady in every position.
quests.hint: 'did' and 'add' end with [d]. Does your voice continue until the very end?
quests.explanation: A final [d] keeps the tongue on the ridge while the voice hums, then stops. The vowel before it stretches slightly longer than before [t].
quests.textToSpeak: Did you add the date to the calendar?
quests.phoneticHint: Compare 'add' [æd] with 'at' [æt]: [d] gives a longer vowel and a voiced closure.
commonMistakes: Turning final [d] into [t], so 'add' sounds like 'at'
Dropping the [d] at the end of 'add'
Using a dental [d] with the tongue between the teeth

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud in a firm, workplace tone.
quests.hint: Listen for [d] in 'should', 'decide', 'today' and twice in 'deadline'.
quests.explanation: In 'deadline' the [d] is released sideways into the [l]: keep the tongue tip on the ridge and just lower its sides.
quests.textToSpeak: We should decide today, before the deadline.
quests.phoneticHint: 'deadline' is [ˈdedlaɪn]: after the second [d], the tongue stays in place for [l], so you hear no vowel between them.

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [k] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: The letter c in 'close' and 'cupboard' makes [k]. 'cupboard' also hides a surprise in the spelling.
quests.explanation: Lift the back of your tongue to touch the soft part of the roof of your mouth, hold the air, then release with a small puff. Voice stays off.
quests.textToSpeak: Close the cupboard before you leave.
quests.phoneticHint: 'cupboard' is [ˈkʌbərd]: the spelling suggests [p], but you say a [b] and no [p].
commonMistakes: Moving the tongue too far forward, so [k] sounds like [t]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [k] steady in every position.
quests.hint: Notice that 'ck' and 'c' both give [k] in 'pack', 'snack', 'jacket' and 'cold'.
quests.explanation: At the end of 'pack' and 'snack' the back of the tongue blocks the air and stops it. Keep the vowel before it short and crisp.
quests.textToSpeak: Pack a snack and a jacket. It gets cold up there.
quests.phoneticHint: Vowels before a voiceless [k] are short: [pæk], [snæk]. A 'ck' spelling never adds a second sound.
commonMistakes: Dropping the final [k], so 'pack' sounds like 'pa'
Turning final [k] into [g], so 'pack' sounds like 'pag'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite phone request.
quests.hint: The word 'clinic' contains [k] at both the beginning and the end.
quests.explanation: Before [l] in 'clinic' and 'close', the back of the tongue is already lifted for [k]; release it straight into the [l] without a vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you call the clinic and ask when they close?
quests.phoneticHint: 'clinic' is [ˈklɪnɪk]: a [k] on each side. In 'ask' [æsk], the [k] follows [s] and ends the word.

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [g] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: [g] begins 'go', 'get' and 'glass'. Feel the buzz in your throat before the vowel.
quests.explanation: Use the same tongue position as [k], back of the tongue on the soft palate, but let your voice hum as you release and add no puff of air.
quests.textToSpeak: Go get a glass of water.
quests.phoneticHint: [g] is the voiced partner of [k]: [goʊ] has a buzz in the throat, [koʊ] has breath.
commonMistakes: Releasing so lightly that [g] becomes a soft rubbing sound

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [g] steady in every position.
quests.hint: 'dog' ends in [g], 'digging' has one in the middle, and 'garden' begins with one. The 'gg' in 'digging' is a single sound.
quests.explanation: In 'digging' the [g] stops the air between two vowels; then '-ing' brings a separate nasal sound, so keep them distinct.
quests.textToSpeak: The dog keeps digging holes in the garden.
quests.phoneticHint: 'digging' is [ˈdɪgɪŋ]: a [g] stop in the middle, then [ɪŋ]. In 'dog' [dɒg], the voice continues through the closure.
commonMistakes: Softening the medial [g] into a rubbing sound

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as if you were on a help-desk call.
quests.hint: 'forgot', 'login' and 'again' all hide a [g] in the middle. Keep it a firm stop each time.
quests.explanation: Between vowels, close the back of the tongue fully and release with voice. If air leaks through, the sound softens and stops being [g].
quests.textToSpeak: I forgot my login again. Could you reset it?
quests.phoneticHint: 'again' is [əˈgen]: the [g] begins the stressed syllable, so it should be clear and firm.
commonMistakes: Softening [g] into a friction sound between vowels

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [m] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: [m] begins 'my', 'mother' and 'made', and it ends 'some'.
quests.explanation: Close your lips, lower the soft palate so air flows through your nose, and let your voice buzz. You should feel your lips tingle.
quests.textToSpeak: My mother made some soup for lunch.
quests.phoneticHint: Hold [mmm] and pinch your nose: the sound stops, because [m] is a nasal.
commonMistakes: Opening the lips too early at the end of 'some', so it drifts toward [n]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [m] steady in every position.
quests.hint: 'come' and 'home' both end in [m]. Close your lips and keep humming.
quests.explanation: For final [m], the lips close while the sound continues through the nose. There is nothing to release, so just open the lips silently.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll come home at seven, then make pasta.
quests.phoneticHint: 'home at' links as [hoʊ.mət]: the [m] slides across to begin the next syllable.
commonMistakes: Dropping the closure and leaving only a nasal vowel

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a workplace question.
quests.hint: [m] appears at the start, middle and end of these words: 'remember', 'number', 'meeting', 'room'.
quests.explanation: In 'remember' and 'number', the lips stay closed while air switches from your nose to a small oral burst for [b].
quests.textToSpeak: Can you remember the number of the meeting room?
quests.phoneticHint: 'number' is [ˈnʌmbər]: the [b] is real and voiced, so don't drop it. 'remember' [rɪˈmembər] has it too.

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [n] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: [n] begins 'not', 'now' and 'next'.
quests.explanation: Touch the tongue tip to the ridge behind the upper teeth, let air flow through your nose, and use your voice. Pinch your nose and the sound should stop.
quests.textToSpeak: Not now, maybe next week.
quests.phoneticHint: [n] uses the same tongue spot as [t] and [d], but the air escapes through the nose instead of as a burst.
commonMistakes: Pronouncing it as [l], so 'now' sounds like 'low'
Touching the teeth rather than the ridge
Leaving the nose closed, so it sounds like [d]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [n] steady in every position.
quests.hint: 'turn', 'on', 'fan' and 'in' all finish with [n]. The tongue stays up.
quests.explanation: For final [n], the tongue tip stays on the ridge while your voice hums through your nose. If the tongue drops, only a vague nasal vowel is left.
quests.textToSpeak: Please turn on the fan. It's hot in here.
quests.phoneticHint: In 'fan' [fæn] the tongue makes contact before the sound ends. Compare 'fang' [fæŋ], where the back of the tongue makes contact instead.
commonMistakes: Replacing final [n] with [ŋ], so 'fan' sounds like 'fang'
Leaving out the tongue contact so only a nasal vowel remains

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would tell a friend.
quests.hint: 'knocked' starts with [n] because the k is silent. Find [n] in 'neighbour', 'knocked', 'and', 'turn' and 'down'.
quests.explanation: English drops the k in 'kn-' spellings, so 'knocked' begins like 'nod'. Then the tongue moves back for [k] before the final [t].
quests.textToSpeak: My neighbour knocked and asked us to turn the music down.
quests.phoneticHint: 'knocked' is [nɒkt]: one syllable ending in [t], not [ɪd].

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [f] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: [f] begins 'first', 'film' and 'four'.
quests.explanation: Rest your upper teeth lightly on your lower lip and blow air through the small gap. There is no voice, just a steady hiss of air.
quests.textToSpeak: The first film starts at four.
quests.phoneticHint: [f] is continuous, so you can hold it: [fffɪrst]. A [p] would stop the air completely.
commonMistakes: Using both lips, so [f] sounds like [p]

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [f] steady in every position.
quests.hint: 'enough' ends with the spelling 'gh' but sounds like [f]; in 'half' the l is silent.
quests.explanation: The final [f] needs the same lip-teeth contact and steady airflow as at the start. Let the air continue until the sound ends.
quests.textToSpeak: We've had enough food, so I'll take half home.
quests.phoneticHint: 'enough' is [ɪˈnʌf] and 'half' is [hæf]: the ending is a short hiss, not a [p] burst.
commonMistakes: Ending 'enough' with a hard [k] or [g] because of the 'gh' spelling

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite refusal.
quests.hint: 'afraid', 'for' and 'friend' all use [f]. In 'afraid' it starts the second syllable.
quests.explanation: The [f] in 'afraid' begins the stressed syllable, so give it the same clear airflow as at the start of 'friend'.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm afraid that seat is for my friend.
quests.phoneticHint: 'afraid' [əˈfreɪd] and 'friend' [frend] both have [fr]: the [f] must finish before the tongue moves for [r].

quests.instruction: Say it slowly first, feeling the [v] each time, then once more at normal speed.
quests.hint: Find [v] in 'have', 'vegetables' and 'every'.
quests.explanation: Use the same lip-on-teeth position as [f], but switch your voice on. You should feel a light buzz on your lower lip.
quests.textToSpeak: I try to have vegetables every day.
quests.phoneticHint: 'vegetables' is [ˈvedʒtəbəlz] and is usually said in three syllables, not four.
commonMistakes: Devoicing to [f] at the end of 'have'

quests.instruction: Read it at a relaxed speed and keep the [v] steady in every position.
quests.hint: The [v] in 'give' and 'Dave' comes at the end of the word: keep your voice on.
quests.explanation: Final [v] needs voicing all the way to the end. The lower lip touches the teeth, air keeps flowing, and the buzz doesn't switch off early.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll give Dave your message when he arrives.
quests.phoneticHint: 'arrives' is [əˈraɪvz]: the [v] joins [z] with no vowel between them.
commonMistakes: Using [b] instead of [v] at the end of 'Dave'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a natural reaction.
quests.hint: 'lovely', 'view', 'I've' and 'never' each contain [v]. In 'never' it sits between two vowels.
quests.explanation: Between vowels, keep the lip-teeth contact and the voice steady; it should not turn into [b] or [w].
quests.textToSpeak: That's a lovely view. I've never seen anything like it.
quests.phoneticHint: 'lovely' is [ˈlʌvli]: [v] follows the stressed vowel. 'view' begins with [vj]: [vjuː].
commonMistakes: Ending 'I've' without the [v], so it sounds like 'I'
